Making an excellent design system legible

A self-initiated study of Stripe's checkout theming. The components held under every stress I could build. What didn't hold was the merchant's view of system. The system enforces limits in design, and does not notify the merchant.

Overview

Most design system case studies are written from a team, that shares a Figma library and a Slack channel. Stripe's checkout ships to thousands of businesses who share none of that. They recolour it, restyle it, and drop it into their own page and they cannot preview it.

At a glance
  • Role: Research, synthesis, user experience, prototyping
  • Type: Self-initiated, no affiliation with Stripe
  • Duration: One week
The problem

Stripe's checkout is the most interesting design system problem I know of. The merchant's designer owns the brand, has a colour and a typeface and a set of rules, and wants the payment step to feel like the rest of the experience. They will never see Stripe's source, and they mostly won't test the checkout in another language.

How I tested it

I gave myself one merchant's brand and tried to break it. I used a sandbox to compare. The sandbox is not a Stripe product but it uses Stripe's test keys to load Stripe's real payment form.

Tests

  • Theme: Hot pink, hard shadows, pill shapes, and a left padding rule written the way an English-speaking office writes one.
  • Typeface: Playfair Display, which has no Arabic letters, against Noto Kufi Arabic and the system font.
  • Language: English, German, Japanese, and Arabic, which reads right to left and mirrors the whole form.
  • Currency: Five, including yen, which has no decimal places, and dinar, which has three.

The biggest gap in this study is that there is no merchant interviews yet. Every claim comes from Stripe's public documentation.

Components

The components are excellent. I could not break them. Arabic and right-to-left, multiple currencies, no-decimal currencies, they all held up. The problems are not in the components. They are in what a merchant can see, and control.

A loud theme, hot pink, hard shadows, pill shapes, still coherent.

The same theme in Arabic. Labels, inputs, tabs, and icons all mirror.

The one exception: a Latin-only font in Arabic. Two typefaces, neither chosen.

Findings

Stripe's system constantly makes decisions on the merchant's behalf. The system is less controllable than they make it to be.

I started this project expecting to redesign components. The actual opportunity arose where a specific theme gets chosen. For hosted Checkout, it previews a single condition. For the embedded form, where most of these findings are, there is no editor at all.

The colour has to be typed in manually, as #FF3D7F. So it now lives in two places. Translucent colours are refused: rgb() is accepted, rgba() is not, so a brand that has overlays has to drop them at the payment step.

What happens next is the checkout still loads, in Stripe's own brand color rather than the merchant's pink, and the only error is a line in the console.

2. Stripe lets a merchant restyle the checkout by naming its pieces: the input boxes, the labels above them, the payment method tabs. Each piece accepts a fixed set of changes, mostly colour, spacing, borders and corner rounding. Ask for anything outside that set and it is dropped. No error, no warning. The form renders as if the instruction was never written.

The limit itself is right. A payment form that a merchant can reshape freely can break easily.

The problem is that merchants are told they can theme their checkout. They are never shown where theming stops, so a designer hands over a spec, a developer writes it, and both assume it shipped but only half of it does.

3. A checkout is not only the merchant's brand. Apple Pay is black, Link is green, Klarna is pink, Amazon is yellow, and Visa, Mastercard and Amex each bring their own mark. None of them can be recoloured, and they should not be: a shopper needs to recognise the button that holds their card. Stripe also adds its own elements, like a green cashback badge on the bank option, which the merchant never asked for and cannot remove.

With card payments only, the checkout looks like the merchant. If a merchant turns on nine payment methods, which any shop selling across Europe does, the page becomes a wall of other companies' logos with the merchant's pink button at the bottom. Nothing changes this and the merchant is given no warning about it.

4. A shopper in Dubai with an English phone taps Arabic on a merchant's site. Everything turns Arabic until the payment step, which stays English. Not because Arabic is unsupported, with the browser set to Arabic the hosted page rendered beautifully. The merchant does not have that option.

The design

Stress preview in the Branding page

Today, Stripe's Branding page shows the merchant's theme in exactly one condition: English, US dollars, card only, desktop. That is the condition least likely to break.

Today. Stripe's Branding page: two colour pickers, one preview, no contrast warning.

The proposal: the same page, with the merchant's theme rendered live in the four conditions nobody tests before launch, right to left, a no-decimal currency, a crowded payment list, phone width. It is buildable with what Stripe already has: the same payment form, rendered four times with different settings.

Typeface coverage

A font picker that knows which languages a merchant serves, and says when a face has no letters for one of them.

The same pattern applies to colour. My own test theme's pink button puts white text at roughly 3.4:1 contrast, under the accessibility standard for body text. The system can already compute this and I got no warning while I was picking it.

Language gap

If the hosted page cannot offer Arabic, the system should say so with an alternative.

Stripe should support the four right-to-left languages on both surfaces. This screen is what I would design temporarily.
